paras: The killing of John Williams by Newport News police took place in Newport News, Virginia, in early August 1900, when Policeman R. B. Payne fired after Williams, a Black man known as "Coffee", as he fled custody after a raid on a craps game. Williams was found dead about an hour later, and Payne was charged with murder. A police court judge dismissed the charge on the ground that an officer may shoot an escaping prisoner, and Payne returned to duty.

According to the Virginian-Pilot's Newport News correspondent, the man known as "Coffee" and three other Black men were playing craps when a sergeant and two officers, one of them Payne, surprised the game. Later reports placed the raid on Saturday night, August 4, while the first dispatch, dated August 6, said the killing happened "last night". One item located the raid "in Rocketts", a place not otherwise identified in the coverage.

On the way to the station-house, "Coffee" broke away, and Payne gave chase. In the officers' version, when the man ignored orders to halt, Payne fired three shots after him, "apparently without effect", and then rejoined the others. An hour later the sergeant came upon the body in a dark corner and had it taken to the station. None of the reports describes the wounds or states the cause of death.

A coroner's inquest was held, and Payne, released on bail, was set for a preliminary hearing. The hearing in Police Court was continued to Thursday morning, August 9. There Judge Brown heard testimony that was the same as at the inquest, along with Payne's own statement, and dismissed the murder charge, after which Payne resumed his place on the force. Judge Brown held that an officer is justified in shooting an escaping prisoner "no matter upon what specific charge the fugitive may have been arrested."

Coverage was slight and came entirely from white papers. The Virginian-Pilot first ran the story as a short paragraph headed "A Negro Killed" at the foot of a Newport News column led by news of a planned steel plant, noting that the victim's "rightful name cannot be learned". Its follow-ups, "Payne Trial Continued" and "Charge Dismissed", referred to him as "the negro Coffee" and "the negro crap player" and gave his name as John Williams only at the dismissal.

The Washington Weekly Post carried the dismissal dispatch under the headline "Policeman Payne Goes Free" and the subhead "Newport News Officer Who Killed Escaping Crap Player Exonerated". Every account relied on the officers' version and the officer's statement in court, and no report gives the account of the other men arrested or of Williams's family. No coverage of the killing was found in the Black press.

The reports differ on the dates: the first dispatch's "last night" points to August 5, while three later items say Saturday night, and the first dispatch's mention of an inquest held "yesterday" fits the earlier date. The Post dated the dismissal August 9, matching the scheduled hearing, while the Pilot of August 11 said it happened "yesterday".

bases: A policeman shot after a man who broke from custody on the way to the station-house after a craps raid, and the man was found dead; no crowd was involved (A1, A3).

Every account of the killing comes from the Virginian-Pilot's Newport News correspondence (A1, A2, A3); the Washington Weekly Post item repeats the same dismissal dispatch nearly word for word (A4), and all versions rest on the officers' account and the officer's statement.

accounts.gist: On testimony the same as at the coroner's inquest and the officer's statement, Judge Brown dismissed the murder charge, holding that an officer is justified in shooting an escaping prisoner.

framing.detail: The Virginian-Pilot ran the killing as a short item headed 'A Negro Killed' in a Newport News column led by news of a steel plant, presenting the officers' version without comment.

The Washington Weekly Post headlined 'Policeman Payne Goes Free' and 'Newport News Officer Who Killed Escaping Crap Player Exonerated', closing on the judge's holding that shooting an escaping prisoner is justified.
The Pilot's follow-ups 'Payne Trial Continued' and 'Charge Dismissed' reported the court steps briefly, calling the victim 'the negro Coffee' and 'the negro crap player'.

conflicts.note: The first dispatch also says an inquest had already been held 'yesterday', which fits a Saturday-night killing better than a Sunday-night one; three later items say Saturday night.
